read.sections.0.text.source: Hội An is a town in central Viet Nam, near the place where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, it was a busy trading port. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded and carried them. The river and the sea connected the town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a visiting trader. Local people built their lives there too. The town's location helps explain why a port grew there. It cannot tell us who had power, or how each family lived.
read.sections.0.text.back: Hội An is a town in central Vietnam, near the place where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, this town was a busy trading port. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded and carried those goods. The river and the sea connected this town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a visiting trader. Local people also built their lives there. This town's location helps explain why a port grew there. Its location cannot tell us who had power, or how each family lived.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Viet Nam" is written "Vietnam", as Malaysian textbooks and news write it.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Hội An is a town in Viet Nam. It is near a river and the sea. For about 400 years, it was a busy port. Boats came with goods. People on land sold and carried the goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local people lived there too. The river helps us see why a port grew here. It does not tell us how each family lived.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Hội An is a town in Vietnam. This town is near a river and the sea. For about 400 years, this town was a busy port. Boats came bringing goods. People on land sold and carried those goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local people also lived there. The river helps us understand why a port grew here. The river does not tell us how each family lived.

read.sections.1.text.source: In 1999, UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, listed Hội An as a World Heritage site. Its description says the old town has shops, homes, an open market and a ferry quay. Many buildings face the street, so customers could walk in. Their backs open to the river, so goods could go on and off boats. From this, we can make an inference: the river and the street were both important for trade. UNESCO says the buildings mix local ways with mostly Chinese and Japanese ideas, and later European ones. This is a modern account, not a diary from a trader in the 1500s.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 1999, UNESCO, part of the United Nations, listed Hội An as a World Heritage Site. Its description states that the old town has shops, homes, an open market and a ferry quay. Many buildings face the street, so that customers could come in. Their back part opens to the river, so that goods could be loaded into boats and unloaded. From this, we can make an inference: the river and the street were both important for trade. UNESCO states that the buildings mix local ways with ideas mostly from China and Japan, and European ideas that came later. This is a modern account, not the diary of a trader in the 1500s.

UNESCO wrote this in modern times. It is not a diary from long ago.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 1999, UNESCO listed Hội An as a special place. UNESCO is part of the United Nations. UNESCO states the town has shops, homes and a market. There is a quay by the river. Customers come in from the front part of a shop. Its back part opens to the river, where boats load goods. So we can make an inference. read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, taken in 2018. The bridge is part of the town's heritage, a place people value and look after today. The photo shows what the bridge looked like on that day. It cannot show the first traders who used the port centuries ago, or what every resident thought. The map helps us see possible connections, and the photo lets us look at a place now. To hear a resident's view from long ago, we would need other sources, such as old records or objects.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, which was taken in 2018. The bridge is part of the town's heritage, that is, a place people value and look after today. The photo shows what the bridge looked like on that day. The photo cannot show the first traders who used the port centuries ago, or what every resident thought. The map helps us see possible connections, and the photo lets us look at a place now. To hear the view of a resident from long ago, we need other sources, such as old records or old objects.

watch.summary.source: This is a short film of a few minutes. NHK, a broadcaster from Japan, made it with UNESCO. It is part of a series of films about World Heritage sites. UNESCO's record of the film says it is about the old town and its covered bridge, often called the Japanese Bridge. The record describes Hội An in a few words. Hội An is an old trading port that has been well looked after. It was a port from the 1400s to the 1800s. Its buildings and its street plan show a mix of local ways and ideas from other places. Remember that a camera films a place on one day. The film shows Hội An in modern times, not the busy port of long ago.
watch.summary.back: This is a short film a few minutes long. NHK, a broadcaster from Japan, made it with UNESCO. This film is part of a series of films about World Heritage Sites. Hội An is an old trading port that has been looked after well. This town was a port from the 1400s to the 1800s. Its buildings and street layout show a mix of local ways and ideas from other places. Remember that a camera films a place on one day. This film shows Hội An in modern times, not the busy port of long ago.

educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: that a later photo is a picture of the port's earlier daily life. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influences" in buildings do not tell us every resident's ancestry, and local people were not passive; the bridge's popular name does not tell us who built or used it. UNESCO's listing dates the wooden bridge, with a pagoda on it, to the 18th century, while other accounts give an earlier first bridge, so the lesson does not date it. Source caveats: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of surviving buildings; the photo shows a lower modern footbridge in front and crowds of visitors in 2018. For an optional comparison with another port that records local voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but do not make it a second case.
educatorNotes.1.back: Misconception to address: that a photo taken later is a picture of the port's earlier daily life. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influences" on buildings do not tell us every resident's ancestry, and local people were not only standing by; the bridge's popular name does not tell us who built or used it. UNESCO's listing states the wooden bridge, which has a pagoda on it, dates from the 18th century, while other accounts give an earlier date for the first bridge, so this lesson does not date the bridge. Source caveats: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of buildings that still exist; the photo shows a lower modern footbridge in front and many visitors in 2018. For an optional comparison with another port that records local voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but do not make it a second case.
educatorNotes.1.note: "local people were not passive" rendered "penduduk tempatan bukan hanya berdiam diri" (were not only staying quiet); a reviewer may prefer "tidak pasif".
